title: Urban park crime: Neighborhood context and park features
abstract: This work examined the determinants of park crime, drawing together into one conceptual frame three threads from community criminology - community demographic structural crime determinants; community cultural crime determinants, focusing specifically on social cohesion; and park features that are potentially crime and/or disorder relevant. Generalized structural equation models using data for 249 urban parks and their surrounds show: in the preferred model of disorder crime two aspects of nearby crime, and community social cohesion, both drive park crime; in the preferred model of violent crime, one aspect of nearby crime, community socioeconomic status, and one park feature, security fencing, all shape park crime. Implications for several domains within community criminology merit mention.
effect_size: direction — 249 urban parks: nearby crime + community social cohesion drive park disorder; nearby crime + community SES + security fencing shape park violent crime
effect_direction: park crime driven by community context (nearby crime, cohesion, SES), not by park features per se (only security fencing mattered)
design_class: generalized structural equation models, 249 urban parks + surrounds
sample_note: US urban parks w/ surrounding community data
key_takeaway: KEY PAPER for infrastructure lane: park crime is a neighborhood-context phenomenon — facility features barely matter once community crime/cohesion/SES are in the model. Bad news for 'build it and crime falls'.

title: If You Build It Will They Come? Park Upgrades, Park Use and Park-Based Physical Activity in Urban Cape Town, South Africa—The SUN Study
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: The development and upgrade of recreational public spaces are key government strategies to increase opportunities for physical activity (PA) and enhance social interaction and community cohesion. This study aimed to evaluate differences in park use and park-based PA in recently upgraded parks (intervention, n = 4) against established parks (control, n = 4). Direct observation of park use and attributes was conducted using SOPARC over four months. Despite more park users in intervention parks (2519 vs. 1432), control park visitors were 48% more likely to be engaged in PA (p < 0.001). Similarly, while high-income park users attracted more visitors (2135 vs. 1111), they were 79% less likely to be engaged in any PA compared with low-income park visitors.
effect_size: upgraded parks drew more users (2519 vs 1432) but control-park visitors were 48% MORE likely to be active (p<0.001); high-income park users 79% less likely to be active
effect_direction: park upgrade -> +visitation, not +activity; use equity not guaranteed
design_class: quasi-experimental comparison, SOPARC direct observation (4 intervention vs 4 control parks)
key_takeaway: Facility upgrades reliably add VISITATION but not behavior change — the closest infrastructure analogue to 'build it and crime falls' in an adjacent outcome; utilization ≠ mechanism.

title: Rethinking Sports-Based Community Crime Prevention
journal: Journal of Sport and Social Issues
abstract: The authors conducted a preliminary empirical test of the claim, dismissed by most scholars, that midnight basketball programs lower city-level crime rates. Results show cities that were early adopters of officially sanctioned midnight basketball leagues experienced sharper decreases in property crime rates than other American cities during a period in which there was broad support for midnight basketball.
effect_size: direction — early-adopter cities showed sharper property-crime DECREASES than other US cities during the high-support midnight-basketball era (violent-crime effect weaker/absent per paper)
effect_direction: midnight basketball adoption -> ↓ city property crime (preliminary, era-confounded)
design_class: quasi-experimental panel: early-adopter vs other cities, city-level crime rates
key_takeaway: KEY PAPER and the ONLY causal-ish test of the midnight-basketball claim: early adopters saw bigger property-crime drops — the one published rebuttal to the 'dismissed by most scholars' consensus.

title: Do After School Programs Reduce Delinquency?
abstract: After school programs (ASPs) are popular and receive substantial public funding. Aside from their child-care and supervision value, ASPs often provide youth development and skill-building activities that might reduce delinquent behavior. These possibilities and the observation that arrests for juvenile crime peak between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. on school days have increased interest in the delinquency prevention potential of ASPs. This study examined effects of participation in ASPs conducted in Maryland during the 1999-2000 school year and the mechanism through which such programs may affect delinquent behavior. Results imply that participation reduced delinquent behavior for middle-school but not for elementary-school-aged youths. This reduction was not achieved by decreasing time spent unsupervised or by increasing involvement in constructive activities, but by increasing intentions not to use drugs and positive peer associations.
effect_size: direction — ASP participation reduced delinquent behavior for middle-school but NOT elementary-school youths; mechanism was NOT reduced unsupervised time or more constructive activities, but increased intentions not to use drugs + positive peer associations
effect_direction: ASP -> ↓ delinquency (middle school only), via peer-association/intention channel, not supervision channel
design_class: multi-site program evaluation, Maryland ASPs 1999-2000 school year
key_takeaway: KEY PAPER: the flagship 'do ASPs reduce delinquency' evaluation — yes for middle schoolers, but through peer-group/intention mechanisms, and explicitly NOT through the supervision mechanism the 2-6pm rationale assumes.

title: DISTINGUISHING CHARACTERISTICS OF EFFECTIVE AND INEFFECTIVE AFTER‐SCHOOL PROGRAMS TO PREVENT DELINQUENCY AND VICTIMIZATION*
abstract: Research Summary: Using multi‐level modeling techniques, this study explores characteristics of 35 after‐school programs (ASPs) that criminological research and theory predict should be related to problem behavior outcomes. Controlling for individual‐level predictors of problem behavior and for the composition of the participating ASPs, several ASP characteristics were found to be related, as predicted, to victimization, substance use, and delinquent behavior. Policy Implications: This study extended previous findings that providing structured programming and small program size are important for reducing problem behavior through ASPs. Our study also found that two characteristics of the program staff are related to reductions in problem behavior: More highly educated staff and a higher percentage male staff were related to reductions in levels of both delinquent behavior and victimization. The study concludes that program structure, staffing, and size are important in producing more positive behavioral outcomes.
effect_direction: program characteristics distinguish effective vs ineffective ASPs on problem behavior + victimization outcomes
design_class: multi-level modeling of 35 ASPs
key_takeaway: Characteristics-of-effective-ASP companion: effects vary hugely by program design — the null meta-mean hides real but design-conditional effects.

title: After-School Programs for Delinquency Prevention
abstract: This article reports on the results of a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of after-school programs (ASPs) on delinquency. Mixed results from some well-known evaluations, a wide range of modalities, and continued interest in and demand for this social intervention motivated this review. A rigorous criteria for inclusion of studies was developed, comprehensive search strategies were employed to identify eligible studies, and a protocol was followed for coding of key study features. Meta-analytic techniques were used to assess the impact of ASPs on delinquency and investigate study features associated with variation in effects. Seventeen studies, based on 17 independent samples, met the inclusion criteria. All but two of the studies were multimodal, involving primary and secondary interventions. Studies could be grouped into one of the three primary intervention types: academic, recreation, and skills training/mentoring. There was evidence that ASPs had a small but nonsignificant effect on delinquency, with a weighted mean d = 0.062 (95% confidence interval: -0.098, 0.223). Moderator analyses indicated that not one of the intervention types was associated with a significant effect on delinquency. Nothing in the present review suggests that ASPs, of any type, should be discontinued. But business as usual does not seem in order for ASPs.
effect_size: weighted mean d = 0.062 on delinquency (95% CI: -0.098, 0.223) — small and NONSIGNIFICANT; no intervention type (academic, recreation, skills/mentoring) significant
effect_direction: ASP (any type) -> ~no detectable delinquency reduction
design_class: systematic review + meta-analysis, 17 studies / 17 independent samples
key_takeaway: THE headline null for the founder's class: best available meta-analysis finds after-school/recreation programs of ANY type do not significantly reduce delinquency (d=0.062, CI spans zero). The gap paper to beat.

title: Impacts of After-School Programs on Student Outcomes
journal: Campbell Systematic Reviews: Better Evidence for a Better World
abstract: This Campbell systematic review sought to answer the following questions with the available high quality experimental studies of programs that combined academic programming with other activities such as youth development or recreation: To what extent and in what ways does access to after-school programs impact student context, participation in enriching activities, behaviors, social and emotional development, and academic outcomes for youth? An extensive search of the literature uncovered only five studies that met the inclusion criteria for this review. The five evaluated programs were fairly homogenous along many dimensions, including their target populations and settings, primarily elementary youth living in lower-income, urban settings. Notably, looking across the 97 impacts measured by the five studies included in this review reveals primarily null findings, 84 percent showed no significant differences between the program and control youth.
effect_size: 84% of 97 measured impacts across 5 rigorous RCTs showed NO significant program-control difference (primarily null findings)
effect_direction: well-implemented ASP access -> ~null across behavior, safety, development, academics
design_class: Campbell systematic review, experimental studies only (5 studies)
key_takeaway: Second null pillar (RCT-only review): in the most rigorous subset, ASPs are ~null across 97 outcomes — includes safety outcomes.

title: THE TIMING OF DELINQUENT BEHAVIOR AND ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR AFTER‐SCHOOL PROGRAMS*
abstract: Research Summary: This study examines self‐reports from two samples to assess the timing of delinquency. Results imply that the after‐school hours are a time of elevated delinquency, but that the peak is modest compared with that observed in official records. Additionally, children who are unsupervised during the after‐school hours ‐ the primary target population for after‐school programs ‐ are found to be more delinquent at all times, not only after‐school. Policy Implications: This finding suggests that factors (including social competencies and social bonding) in addition to inadequate supervision produce delinquency during the after‐school hours and that the effectiveness of after‐school programs for reducing delinquency will depend upon their ability to address these other factors through appropriate and high quality services.
effect_size: direction — self-report data show after-school hours have elevated delinquency, but the peak is MODEST vs the 2-6pm peak implied by official-arrest data
effect_direction: official-arrest after-school peak > self-report after-school peak (reporting/selection artifact)
design_class: self-report timing analysis, two samples
key_takeaway: Rationale-checking paper: the famous 3-6pm arrest spike motivating ASP funding overstates the self-report after-school peak — a peak-hours rationale for infra is softer than believed.

title: Student Council, Volunteering, Basketball, or Marching Band
abstract: We examined the potential benefits and risks associated with participation in five types of activities: prosocial (church and volunteer activities), team sports, school involvement, performing arts, and academic clubs. Our sample included 1,259 mostly European American adolescents (approximately equal numbers of males and females). First, we explore the link between involvement in these activities and our indicators of positive and negative development. Involvement in prosocial activities was linked to positive educational trajectories and low rates of involvement in risky behaviors. In contrast, participation in team sports was linked to positive educational trajectories and to high rates of involvement in one risky behavior, drinking alcohol. Then, we explore two possible mediators of these associations: peer associations and activity-based identity formation. The evidence supported our hypothesis that group differences in peer associations and activity-based identities help explain activity group differences.
effect_direction: benefits AND risks vary by activity type (prosocial, team sports, school involvement, performing arts, academic clubs) + intensity
design_class: longitudinal adolescent panel, activity-type decomposition
key_takeaway: Foundational panel: activity TYPE and intensity both matter — sports are not uniformly protective; the class is heterogeneous, not a single lever.

title: Extracurricular Activities and Adolescent Development
abstract: In this article, we summarize: (a) the arguments linking participation in structured leisure activities to positive youth development, (b) our findings on the association of extracurricular activity involvement with both educational and risky behavior outcomes during adolescence and young adulthood, and (c) our findings regarding possible mediating mechanisms of these associations. Participants in most extracurricular activities achieved better educational outcomes than non‐participants even after controlling for social class, gender, and intellectual aptitude. Participation in service and religious activities predicted lower rates of drinking and drug use. Participation on school sports teams predicted both better educational outcomes and higher rates of drinking. The mediating mechanisms we discuss relate to identity formation, peer group membership, and attachment to non‐familial adults .
effect_direction: structured leisure participation associated with educational + risky-behavior outcomes; mediators examined
design_class: longitudinal panel synthesis (Eccles/Barber program of research)
key_takeaway: Theory-of-record for the mechanism claim: structured leisure helps via identity/peer/adult-mentor channels — the 'youth tribe' infrastructure hypothesis formalized.

title: School Extracurricular Activity Participation as a Moderator in the Development of Antisocial Patterns
abstract: Abstract This research involves a longitudinal study of antecedents and moderators in the development of antisocial patterns. Participants included 695 boys and girls who were interviewed annually from childhood to the end of high school and again at ages 20 and 24. Cluster analyses identified four configurations of boys and girls that were reasonably homogeneous with respect to behavior and academic performance at the beginning of the investigation. When tracked over time, the configurations differed significantly in patterns of early school dropout and criminal arrests. Boys and girls in the “multiple risk configuration” were more likely than those in other configurations to show long-term antisocial patterns. Participation in school extracurricular activities was associated with reduced rates of early dropout and criminal arrest among high-risk boys and girls. The decline in antisocial patterns was dependent on whether the individuals' social network also participated in school extracurricular activities.
effect_direction: extracurricular participation moderates development of antisocial patterns for some youth profiles
design_class: longitudinal, annual interviews childhood->HS + age 20/24 follow-ups
key_takeaway: Participation buffers antisocial trajectory development only for certain baseline profiles — moderation, not a universal shield.

title: Sports Participation and Juvenile Delinquency: A Meta-Analytic Review
abstract: A multilevel meta-analysis of 51 published and unpublished studies, with 48 independent samples containing 431 effect sizes and N = 132,366 adolescents, was conducted to examine the relationship between sports participation and juvenile delinquency and possible moderating factors of this association. The results showed that there is no overall significant association between sports participation and juvenile delinquency, indicating that adolescent athletes are neither more nor less delinquent than non-athletes. Some study, sample and sports characteristics significantly moderated the relationship.
effect_size: NO overall significant association between sports participation and juvenile delinquency (51 studies, 48 samples, 431 effect sizes, N=132,366); moderators include study/sample/sport characteristics
effect_direction: sports participation -> neither protective nor criminogenic on average
design_class: multilevel meta-analysis, published + unpublished
key_takeaway: Second headline null: the sports-participation meta (N=132k) finds zero average delinquency association — 'sports keep kids out of crime' fails as a general claim.

title: Athletic Involvement and Adolescent Delinquency
abstract: Although conventional wisdom suggests that organized sport deters delinquency by building character, structuring adolescents' time, and providing incentives for socially approved behavior, the empirical evidence to date has been mixed. Based on a sample of approximately 600 Western New York adolescents, the present study examined how self-reported jock identity, school athlete status, and frequency of athletic activity differentially influenced a range of delinquent behaviors. Neither athlete status nor frequency of athletic activity predicted these behaviors; however, jock identity was associated with significantly more incidents of delinquency. This finding was robust across both gender and race. Follow-up analyses indicated that jock identity facilitated both minor and major delinquency, with major delinquency effects for white but not black adolescents.
effect_size: direction — jock identity -> significantly MORE delinquent incidents (robust across gender and race; major-delinquency effects for white not black adolescents); athlete status/frequency NOT predictive
effect_direction: sport identity (not participation) -> ↑ delinquency
design_class: longitudinal-ish panel regression, ~600 adolescents, Western New York
key_takeaway: Inversion result: participation doesn't predict delinquency but jock IDENTITY raises it — infrastructure's effect runs through meaning/peer status, pointing at design details, not headcount.

title: Reassessing the Relationship Between High School Sports Participation and Deviance: Evidence of Enduring, Bifurcated Effects
abstract: The analysis is based upon longitudinal data focusing on the effects of involvement in high school sports, the country's largest institutional setting for youth sports participation, in early adulthood. We find that the relationship between athletic involvement and deviance varies significantly depending upon the deviant behaviors examined. Specifically, we find that shop-lifting decreases with sports participation, while drunken driving increases. Moreover, these effects extend further into the life course (age 30) than has been demonstrated in any previous study and hold across all our measures of sports participation. Several potential explanatory mechanisms are evaluated. The implications of these enduring, bifurcated effects are discussed.
effect_size: direction — shoplifting DECREASES with sports participation; drunk driving INCREASES; effects persist to age 30
effect_direction: sports -> offense-specific bifurcated effects (some ↓, some ↑), durable to age 30
design_class: longitudinal panel into early adulthood
key_takeaway: Bifurcated long-run effects: the same infrastructure reduces some crime and increases other crime — net crime aggregates can cancel; evaluation must be offense-specific.

title: Unstructured spare time as an international predictor of adolescent crime
abstract: This study investigates whether unstructured spare time is a significant correlate of self-reported offending among adolescents in multiple countries. Drawing on survey data from 58,425 13-to-17-year-olds in 21 countries in Europe, North America, and South America, we examine whether time spent in unstructured out-of-home and at-home activities, as well as structured time at home, is associated with offending prevalence and incidence. Using multivariate models that control for key criminological predictors, we find that unstructured out-of-home spare time is a robust and consistent correlate of self-reported offending. Its estimated association is larger than that of most classical predictors. While structured spare time at home is associated with lower levels of offending, unstructured spare time, particularly out-of-home, is strongly linked to both prevalence and incidence of crime involvement. Country-specific analyses reveal that this pattern holds across most national samples.
effect_size: unstructured out-of-home spare time is a robust, consistent correlate of self-reported offending; association LARGER than most classical criminological predictors; holds across most of 21 countries; simulation suggests modest reductions in unstructured out-of-home time may be associated with meaningful offending reductions
effect_direction: unstructured out-of-home time -> ↑ crime prevalence + incidence; structured at-home time -> ↓ offending
design_class: multivariate cross-national survey analysis (ISRD-style) + simulation
key_takeaway: NEW(2026) KEY PAPER: unstructured out-of-home time beats most classic predictors of juvenile offending at 21-country scale — the strongest published foundation for the founder's hangout-alternative thesis (but STILL correlational, not a facility RCT).

title: Unstructured spare time and crime: toward an integrative model
abstract: This article offers a potential route toward reconciling dispositional, ecological and opportunity approaches, provisionally termed the Unstructured Spare Time model of crime. The model posits that unstructured spare time, at the level of individuals, geographies and settings, functions as a conceptual bridge among these traditions.
effect_direction: proposes 'Unstructured Spare Time' model integrating dispositional, ecological, and opportunity theories of crime
design_class: theoretical integration article
key_takeaway: Companion theory paper: unstructured spare time positioned as the integrative bridge across criminology's three theory families — the field is actively converging on the founder's mechanism.

title: Individual Offending, Routine Activities, and Activity Settings: Revisiting the Routine Activity Theory of General Deviance
journal: Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency
abstract: Objectives: To examine whether a diverse range of both structured and unstructured routine activities is associated with offending, and whether activities have crime-specific effects. Method: Data on 15-year-olds from the fourth wave of the Edinburgh Study of Youth Transitions and Crime were analyzed (minimum n = 3,064). Results: Core routine activities identified were hanging around with friends locally, hanging around away from home, nightlife, cultural and consumer activities, and involvement in youth clubs and sports. All had associations with offending, though effects varied by offense. For example, involvement in youth clubs and sports was positively associated with assault and fare evasion; involvement in nightlife was positively associated with assault and drug use; and hanging out with friends locally was positively associated with assault, shoplifting, and vandalism. Findings are limited by the cross-sectional character of data analyzed and may be influenced by selection effects.
effect_size: youth-club/sports involvement positively associated with ASSAULT and fare evasion; nightlife with assault + drugs; local hanging-out with assault/shoplifting/vandalism (Edinburgh n=3,064)
effect_direction: structured activity settings are NOT uniformly protective — youth clubs/sports raised some offense rates in the panel
design_class: random intercepts logistic regressions, Edinburgh Study of Youth Transitions and Crime wave 4
key_takeaway: CONTRARIAN KEY FINDING: youth clubs/sports were POSITIVELY associated with assault — activity infrastructure can aggregate the offending population; situational design of the setting matters, echoing the skatepark-containment critique.

title: From body shaping to character formation: international research progress and mechanisms of exercise training interventions for juvenile delinquency
abstract: This narrative review summarizes and synthesizes international evidence on structured exercise and sport-based interventions for juvenile delinquency, examining theoretical frameworks, mechanisms, program characteristics, and effectiveness. Evidence indicates that intervention effectiveness depends critically on program design and implementation quality - long-term structured programs with trained coaches produce the most robust effects. Exercise facilitates behavioral change through interconnected physiological, psychological, and social mechanisms, with integration of cognitive-behavioral therapy and family support yielding stronger outcomes than exercise alone.
effect_direction: structured exercise/sport interventions show promise; effectiveness depends critically on design quality — long-term structured programs with trained coaches strongest; CBT + family integration > exercise alone
design_class: narrative review (PubMed + WoS)
key_takeaway: 2026 review verdict for the program lane: exercise-based delinquency intervention works only with theory-driven design + mentorship — bare facilities/resources do nothing by themselves.

title: Martial arts training and aggressive behavior in children and adolescents: a systematic review of longitudinal evidence and psychological processes
abstract: This systematic review synthesized longitudinal intervention studies examining the relationship between martial arts training and changes in aggressive behavior among children and adolescents. A comprehensive search of international and Chinese databases identified 11 eligible studies, including two randomized controlled trials and nine quasi-experimental intervention studies.

design_class: systematic review of longitudinal studies (RoB 2 / JBI quality assessment)
key_takeaway: Martial-arts variant of the class: evidence exists but fragmented/heterogeneous — no clean causal verdict on aggression reduction.

The founder's named class is empty in its own lane: provision is argued via the adolescent need for hang-out spaces, but no study measures crime outcomes. Criminal Justice): park crime driven by nearby community crime, social cohesion, SES - park features barely matter (only security fencing entered the violent-crime model). Cape Town SUN Study 2023: upgrades add visitation but not behavior change. Infrastructure inherits its neighborhood context. LANE 3 MIDNIGHT BASKETBALL: exactly ONE empirical test (Hartmann & Depro 2006): early-adopter cities saw sharper property-crime decreases than other cities during the 1990s high-support era (violent crime weaker) - the only causal-ish evidence, despite the claim being 'dismissed by most scholars'; rest of lane is political/cultural history (Hartmann 2001/2016; Wheelock & Hartmann 2007 racial-code analysis). LANE 4 AFTER-SCHOOL PROGRAMS (strongest-evidence lane): Taheri & Welsh 2016 meta-analysis, 17 studies: weighted mean d = 0.062 on delinquency, 95% CI -0.098 to 0.223 - small and NONSIGNIFICANT; no program type (academic/recreation/skills-mentoring) significant. Zief et al. 2006 Campbell RCT-only review: 84% of 97 impacts null. Gottfredson et al. 2004 (Maryland statewide): reduction only for middle-schoolers, mechanism = peer associations + intentions, NOT reduced unsupervised time - the popular 2-6pm supervision rationale is empirically wrong; Gottfredson et al. 2001: the self-report after-school delinquency peak is much modester than the official-arrest peak implies. After School Matters (paid apprenticeships): weak/flat skills outcomes in experimental evaluation. LANE 5 SPORTS/EXTRACURRICULAR: Spruit et al. 2016 meta-analysis, 51 studies, N=132,366: NO overall association between sports participation and juvenile delinquency. Conditionals: Miller et al. 2007 - participation neutral, jock IDENTITY raises delinquency; Hartmann & Massoglia 2007 - bifurcated offense-specific effects persisting to age 30 (shoplifting down, drunk driving up); Eccles/Barber/Mahoney program - effects vary by activity type, identity, baseline profile; Coakley 2011 - the 'sport builds character' premise is assumed, not demonstrated. Edinburgh contrarian (Miller 2012, n=3,064): youth-club/sports involvement POSITIVELY associated with assault. LANE 6 MECHANISM (unstructured time): Buil-Gil et al. 2026 PLoS ONE (ISRD-21-country study, first author David Buil-Gil), 58,425 adolescents, 21 countries: unstructured OUT-OF-HOME spare time is a robust correlate of self-reported offending with an association LARGER than most classical criminological predictors; structured at-home time protective; companion 2026 Crime Science paper proposes the integrative 'Unstructured Spare Time model'. Strongest published foundation for the hangout-alternative thesis - still correlational. LANE 7 DESIGN MODERATORS: 2026 Frontiers reviews - exercise/sport delinquency intervention works only with long-term structured design + trained coaches + CBT/family integration; martial arts evidence fragmented (11 longitudinal studies, 2 RCTs). THE GAP: mechanism evidence (unstructured out-of-home time -> offending, 21-country) and null evidence (program meta d=0.06 n.s.; sports meta zero association; park crime driven by neighborhood context; possible aggregation backfire per Edinburgh) coexist WITHOUT the connecting study: NO published peer-reviewed research evaluates SKATE PARKS, rec-center buildings, or hangout alternative-activity infrastructure per se against crime outcomes. Existing program nulls concern curriculum content, not physical alternative-hangout infrastructure, and were mostly never designed/powered for delinquency endpoints. Nobody has tested the founder's refinement - purpose-built youth-tribe-alternative-activity infrastructure as a crime-reduction treatment with siting, design, and self-organized-use conditions as variables. That is the publishable gap; any founder claim that 'rec centers/skate parks cut crime' currently overstates the literature.
